title: contextual-sparsity-sketches-ramya-2026-09-22
content:
Quick sketch: contextual sparsity for KV-cache + token importance scheduling

Goal / intuition
- Try a lightweight controller that masks KV entries based on recent token importance rather than strict recency. Idea: not all recent tokens are equally helpful; some earlier tokens (e.g., named entities, instructions) matter more across long sessions.
- Use a combined score per KV row: (recency_decay * recency_weight) + (salience_score * salience_weight) + (topic_persistence * persistence_weight). Then sparsify rows below a threshold before sending to attention.

Why this might help Redwood product use cases
- Dedicated & Private customers often push long context chains (docs + chat). If we can drop 30–60% of KV rows without harming quality in majority of queries, we reduce memory bandwidth and attention compute for long sequences. That improves latency and cost.

Related reading (quick notes)
- "Learned Sparse Attention for Long Contexts" (arXiv:2601.XXXX) — proposes gating per key with small controller net; shows good quality/compute tradeoffs on retrieval-augmented tasks. Key takeaway: a shallow 2-layer gating net trained to predict per-token future attention can zero out many keys with low overhead.
- "Token Importance Distillation" (ICML 2025 workshop) — distill teacher model attention into a light scorer, trained on sampled contexts. Works well as a proxy for salience.
- "KV Mixture-of-Experts" (NeurIPS 2026 short) — shard keys into buckets by semantic hash, then route only top-k buckets for a request. Interesting idea but routing overhead can be nontrivial for low-latency SLOs.

Open design choices (brainstorm)
- Scorer architecture: tiny MLP over key vector vs. separate transformer probe over the last N tokens. Tradeoff: MLP cheap, probe higher precision.
- Training signal: distill from teacher attention (self-attention weights aggregated), or use downstream loss (harder, slower). Distillation seems the pragmatic first step.
- Thresholding policy: static percentile, learned threshold (per-request), or budgeted selection (keep top B rows). Budgeted selection easier to reason about for latency SLOs.
- Incorporate routing fallback: if scorer is uncertain (entropy high), fall back to full attention to avoid catastrophic quality drop.

Experiment plan (minimal viable experiment)
1) Dataset and tasks: use internal long-context eval set (10k examples) combining doc QA, multi-turn chat with long memory, and retrieval-augmented summarization. Evaluate EM/F1 for QA, ROUGE/semantic embedding sim for summary, and human preference proxies for chat.
2) Baselines: full KV (no sparsity), recency-only top-B (naive), and LRU eviction at chunk granularity.
3) Model variant: scorer = 2-layer MLP (64 hidden) taking per-key summary vector (pooled last-layer activation). Distillation target = normalized future attention mass from teacher over next 128 tokens. Train on sampled windows from existing logs.
4) Metrics: task quality delta vs baseline, %KV rows pruned, end-to-end latency p50/p95 on dedicated GPU, memory footprint, compute (FLOPs estimate). Monitor hallucination proxies for QA.
5) Safety net: route any request where pruned rows > 40% and scorer uncertainty high to full model.

Small checklist for prototype run
- [ ] extract 100k training windows from logs (owner: Owen)
- [ ] implement scorer MLP and distillation loss in training harness (owner: Ramya)
- [ ] add gating op to serving runtime (fast bool mask + compact copy) — necessary in C++ runtime path (owner: infra/serving runtime, contact Mika)
- [ ] add telemetry: per-request pruned_count, scorer_entropy, fallback_flag, and quality-sampler hook
- [ ] run offline eval and collect p50/p95 latency delta on dedicated pool

Potential pitfalls / notes to watch
- Distribution shift: scorer trained on historical logs may over-prune on new types of prompts (e.g., code generation with long repeated context), so conservative thresholds initially.
- Edge-case tokens: rare tokens like dates and URIs can be extremely informative but low on learned salience — consider a rule to always keep last N tokens and any token with entity tag.
- Cost of masking: copying KV into compact array may itself be overhead; need to microbenchmark memory bandwidth vs attention savings.

Ideas for rapid variations (to try in parallel)
- Salience heuristics hybrid: token-type signals (ENTITY, CODE, TITLE) + MLP score.
- Lightweight chunk-level scorer: instead of per-token, score chunks of 64 tokens to reduce decision overhead.
- Online adaptive threshold: budget consumption controller that keeps average pruned fraction near a target; update threshold using EWMA.

Notes to self from Slack / PR context
- Slack thread: #kv-sparsity, pinned: initial synthetic results show 12% latency cut at 20% prune with <0.5% QA loss (opaque evaluation). Need reproducibility.
- PR reference: github.com/redwood-inference/contextual-sparsity-experiments PR #7 has training and eval scripts; review commit by Mika on 2026-09-24 (comment: "microbenchmark memory copy costs").

Key questions to resolve before next checkpoint (2026-10-06)
- How to pick the training target window length for distillation (32 vs 128 vs 512)? Impact on scorer generality.
- What is an acceptable fallback rate (we have SLA; too many fallbacks defeats cost goal).
- Where to place gating op in pipeline for minimal extra allocations? In-place mask vs build compact KV slice.

Quick timeline (2-week sprint idea)
- Week 1: data extraction + baseline microbenchmarks (memory copy vs attention ops) + basic scorer training on 100k windows.
- Week 2: integrate gating in local runtime, offline eval on 10k long-context dev set, gather metrics. Decide go/no-go.

To-do (short)
- Ramya: write up prototype runbook and perf checklist (this doc -> confluence)
- Owen: hand off sampled windows export (s3://redwood-experiments/contextual-sparsity/raw/)
- Mika: estimate cost/time to add gating op to dedicated runtime branch
- Team: schedule 30-min sync Mon 2026-09-29 to align on thresholds and telemetry

Random notes / heuristics to remember
- Always keep last M tokens (experiment M in {16, 32})
- Prefer budgeted top-B selection over absolute threshold for predictable latency
- Consider lightweight entity recognizer tag as cheap guard for rare but important tokens

End of sketch. Revisit after initial microbenchmarks.
